Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention
via Structure-Aware Kernels

 

Delyan Boychev 1  Ivo Petrov 1  Dimitar I. Dimitrov 1 

††footnotetext: 1INSAIT, Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski”. Correspondence to: Delyan Boychev <delyan.boychev@insait.ai>.
Preprint. Under review.
Abstract

Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content–position or bias–position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query–relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8–6.4×\times (2.0–21×\times) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9–128×\times (1.4–54×\times) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8×\times faster and uses 2.4×\times less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

1 Introduction

The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) has revolutionized modern machine learning, from large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing to foundation models in speech, vision, and biology. At its core is the scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) mechanism, which allows input tokens to directly attend to each other and aggregate mutual information. However, scaling these models to larger inputs introduces two fundamental challenges, namely injecting scalable positional information into the network, and keeping the computation and memory footprint of SDPA tractable despite its quadratic complexity.

For standard content-based attention, IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024) resolved the quadratic memory bottleneck by streaming blocks of tokens through fast on-chip SRAM, avoiding the materialization of the full N×NN\times N score matrix in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Paired with parameter-free, token-wise rotary position embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), which can be seamlessly integrated into fused kernels, this pipeline now serves as the backbone of most autoregressive LLMs.

Relative-position attention

Parameter-free positional encodings, such as RoPE and ALiBi (Press et al., 2022), are not without drawbacks. Despite their computational efficiency, they often fail to use context beyond the sequence lengths seen during training (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Hua et al., 2025), where learned relative biases such as T5’s generalize better (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). Consequently, learnable relative-position encodings remain an enticing alternative for Transformer models. This class of mechanisms additively augments attention scores with learnable terms that depend on the relative distance i−ji-j between query and key tokens, either through content-to-position projections or scalar biases. This allows modeling explicit, shift-invariant relationships across sequences, and has remained enticing for speech models (Barrault et al., 2023; Sekoyan et al., 2025; Abouelenin et al., 2025), text encoding (He et al., 2023; Zaratiana et al., 2025), proteomics (Elnaggar et al., 2022), and genomics (Linder et al., 2025).

Efficiency limitations of relative-position attention

Despite their modeling advantages, relative-position attention mechanisms are largely incompatible with standard fused attention kernels. Training or running inference with these models typically requires materializing the full N×NN\times N additive position matrix in HBM, reintroducing the exact memory-bandwidth bottleneck that FlashAttention was designed to eliminate. Programmable attention frameworks such as FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2025) offer a partial solution by fusing user-defined per-score callbacks and enabling limited precomputation; however, they still suffer from redundant computation, repeated memory lookups, and atomic contention during backpropagation. Lacking efficient kernels, practitioners often resort to replacing relative-position encodings entirely and retraining models from scratch, as seen in Flashzoi (Hingerl et al., 2025) and FlashSwin (Kataria et al., 2026), or switch to RoPE-based alternatives such as ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2025).

Our work

To address these limitations, we introduce an exact algorithm for relative-position mechanisms. Rather than treating pairwise offsets as opaque per-element lookups, our method exploits the block-level structure of relative distances across the attention matrix (Fig. 1a). Specifically, our method projects queries and keys only onto the offset ranges reachable within each token block (Fig. 1b), structures tile traversal around constant- and variable offset regions to maximize data reuse and avoid redundant indexing (Fig. 1c), and shards backward gradient accumulation by offset to eliminate atomic contention entirely (Fig. 1d).

Empirically, our method substantially reduces both runtime and memory consumption across forward and backward passes in production speech and text models. Our kernels significantly outperform generalist and specialized implementations, as well as state-of-the-art frameworks such as FlexAttention, FlashAttention-4 (Zadouri et al., 2026), and FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025), even when those frameworks are augmented with our preprojected relation decomposition. In particular, for 8​K8\text{K}-token sequences, our method beats the strongest baseline for each mechanism by 1.8–6.4×\times in the forward pass and 2.0–21×\times in the backward pass, while reducing peak memory usage by 2.9–128×\times and 1.4–54×\times, respectively. Applied end-to-end to long-context speech transcription, it delivers a 1.8×\times speedup and 2.4×\times lower memory consumption on Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (Sekoyan et al., 2025), enabling significantly more efficient deployment and training.

Key contributions

Our main contributions include:

  • •

    A unified formulation of additive relative-position attention spanning four mechanisms, exposing shared structure amenable to kernel-level optimization.

  • •

    An exact, drop-in tiled algorithm for fast and memory-efficient relative-position attention.

  • •

    High-performance implementations of our method, validated against a high-precision reference, and comprehensive evaluations across diverse model architectures, sequence lengths, and NVIDIA GPU architectures.

2 Related Work

In this section, we describe relevant prior work on optimizing standard attention and programmable backends for non-standard attention mechanisms. We then describe the uses of relative-position attention and their limitations due to the lack of general optimization algorithms.

2.1 Optimizing Standard Attention

Modern Transformer architectures rely on scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) (Vaswani et al., 2017). However, naive implementations materialize the full attention score and probability matrices in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), incurring storage and I/O costs that grow quadratically with sequence length. To mitigate this bottleneck, Milakov & Gimelshein (2018) introduced an online softmax formulation that processes inputs in column-wise chunks, enabling exact attention computation in sub-quadratic memory (Rabe & Staats, 2021). FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) combines this with IO-aware tiling in on-chip memory, recomputing attention tiles during the backward pass instead of storing large intermediate matrices. FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) restructures the schedule to improve parallelism and reduce overhead by parallelizing the forward pass over query blocks and the backward pass over key blocks. FlashAttention-3 and -4 (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026) further specialize this pipeline for newer GPUs.

Existing kernels target content-based attention and cannot fuse learnable relative-position terms or their gradients. Our method bridges this gap by extending tiled execution to relative-position attention by restricting projections to reachable offsets, reusing them on constant-offset tiles, and using a two-pass backward schedule (Triton Contributors, 2024) for atomic-free gradient accumulation.

2.2 Programmable and Specialized Backends

To support attention variants without hand-writing a kernel per model, recent frameworks expose programmable interfaces that preserve FlashAttention’s optimizations. FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2025) compiles user-defined mask predicates and elementwise score modifications into fused tiled kernels, automatically deriving their backward pass. FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025), AttentionEngine (Chen et al., 2025), and Flashlight (You et al., 2025) provide similar customization through templates or compilers, while others target variant families such as sparse masks (Wang et al., 2025) or low-rank biases (Wu et al., 2025).

Because these frameworks express score modifications as pointwise callbacks on query–key pairs, they can only support relative-position terms via elementwise lookups into precomputed tables. Because this abstraction hides the tile structure, it cannot exploit spatial locality across constant-offset pairs, leading to redundant memory accesses during the forward pass and contention-heavy atomic additions (Dong et al., 2025) during gradient accumulation.

2.3 Relative-Position Attention

Applications of relative-position attention

While modern autoregressive language models largely rely on fixed positional schemes like RoPE (Su et al., 2024) and ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) that integrate neatly into standard SDPA kernels, many domains benefit from expressive, learnable relative-position encodings that inject pairwise token distances directly into the attention logits. Introduced by Shaw et al. (2018), this approach projects queries onto learned embeddings of clipped relative offsets. Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019) expands this notion by incorporating unclipped offsets with learned query biases, DeBERTa (He et al., 2021; He et al., 2023) by modelling both content-to-position and position-to-content interactions, and T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) by mapping offsets to learned scalar bucket biases. Today, these mechanisms remain foundational for long-context modeling across speech, text, and biology. They support the backbone of conformer-based (Gulati et al., 2020) speech and multimodal models such as Parakeet, Canary, SeamlessM4T v2, and Phi-4-multimodal (Sekoyan et al., 2025; Barrault et al., 2023; Abouelenin et al., 2025), DeBERTa-based text and extraction pipelines (Zaratiana et al., 2025), and biological sequence models in proteomics and genomics (Elnaggar et al., 2022; Avsec et al., 2021; Linder et al., 2025). Our method unifies the common computational patterns across all these architectures, providing a single hardware-efficient algorithm.

Optimizing relative-position attention

Despite their widespread adoption, these architectures remain difficult to scale due to the overhead of computing and applying relative-position terms. Early implementations reduced the cost of positional projections by evaluating query- and key-relation dot products once per unique offset, and then mapping the resulting table via explicit index lookups (He et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021) or row-shifting reshape operations (Huang et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2019). However, both strategies still materialize a dense quadratic bias matrix in HBM. Subsequent systems have attempted to fuse this pipeline, though they remain either incomplete or model-specific. For instance, TensorRT’s DeBERTa plugin (NVIDIA, 2022) and NeMo’s Transformer-XL path (Kuchaiev et al., 2019) fuse the offset-gather step yet still materialize the full score matrix in HBM. On the other hand, FlashDeBERTa (Knowledgator, 2025) and GLiNER4j (Gravitee, 2026) integrate positional terms directly into tiled FlashAttention-style kernels (the latter for inference only), but are strictly tailored to DeBERTa. Lacking general kernel support, practitioners often modify and retrain the model instead: Flashzoi (Hingerl et al., 2025) replaces relative-position encodings with RoPE, with analogous replacements appearing for speech recognition (Zhang et al., 2025) and proposed for vision Transformers (Kataria et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Others turn to kernelized attention to incorporate relative positions in sub-quadratic time (Luo et al., 2021; Liutkus et al., 2021), but sacrificing exactness, which has unclear performance impact. Our method accelerates both training and inference across the full family of relative-position architectures without compromising model fidelity or numerical exactness.

3 Background

In this section, we introduce the necessary background for understanding our work. We first recall the definition of standard SDPA and how FlashAttention-1 (Dao et al., 2022) and -2 (Dao, 2024) optimize it. We then define a unified notion of relative–position attention, and explain the drawbacks of existing implementations. We include a full table of the notations used in our paper in App. A for convenience.

3.1 Standard Efficient Attention

We consider a self-attention block for a single sequence of length NN and a single attention head of dimension dd, since batches and heads are computed independently. It takes query, key, and value matrices Q,K,V∈ℝN×dQ,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} with row vectors qi⊤,kj⊤,vj⊤q_{i}^{\top},k_{j}^{\top},v_{j}^{\top} (i,j∈{0,…,N−1}i,j\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}) and computes the output O∈ℝN×dO\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} with rows oi⊤o_{i}^{\top}:

S=τ​Q​K⊤+M,P=softmaxrow⁡(S),O=P​V.S=\tau QK^{\top}+M,\qquad P=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S),\qquad O=PV. (1)

Here τ\tau is a normalization scalar, typically d−12d^{-\frac{1}{2}}, M∈{0,−∞}N×NM\in\{0,-\infty\}^{N\times N} is the additive attention mask, S,P∈ℝN×NS,P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} are the complete softmax logits and row-normalized probabilities, respectively, and softmaxrow\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}} operates row-wise: Pi​j=exp⁡(Si​j)/∑t=0N−1exp⁡(Si​t)P_{ij}=\exp(S_{ij})/\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}\exp(S_{it}).

For any tensor or scalar XX, we denote the gradient of the training loss with respect to XX as d​XdX. Given the incoming output gradient d​O∈ℝN×ddO\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, the backward pass computes the input gradients d​Q,d​K,d​V∈ℝN×ddQ,dK,dV\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}. Differentiating O=P​VO=PV yields d​V=P⊤​d​OdV=P^{\top}dO and d​P=d​O​V⊤dP=dOV^{\top}, which propagate to d​S=P⊙(d​P−D​𝟏⊤)dS=P\odot(dP-D\mathbf{1}^{\top}), where D∈ℝND\in\mathbb{R}^{N} has entries Di=⟨d​Oi,oi⟩D_{i}=\langle dO_{i},o_{i}\rangle. Tiled execution

Materializing the intermediate matrices SS and PP in HBM requires O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) workspace, which causes slow reads and writes, even though neither is needed once OO is produced. FlashAttention-1 and -2 eliminate this bottleneck by partitioning sequences into query tiles ℐ\mathcal{I} and key tiles 𝒥\mathcal{J}—sets of consecutive positions processed together in on-chip SRAM. It parallelizes the forward pass over query tiles: each thread block loads one query tile QℐQ_{\mathcal{I}} and iterates over key and value tiles (K𝒥,V𝒥)(K_{\mathcal{J}},V_{\mathcal{J}}). For each query, it keeps a running maximum mim_{i}, denominator sum ℓi\ell_{i}, and unnormalized output ui∈ℝdu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. At each step 𝒥\mathcal{J}, it computes the score tile Sℐ​𝒥=τ​Qℐ​K𝒥⊤+Mℐ​𝒥S_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}}=\tau Q_{\mathcal{I}}K_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}+M_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} on-chip and updates the state via online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018):

mi′\displaystyle m_{i}^{\prime} =max(mi,maxj∈𝒥Si​j),ℓi′=emi−mi′ℓi+∑j∈𝒥eSi​j−mi′,\displaystyle=\max\!\big(m_{i},\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}}S_{ij}\big),\quad\ell_{i}^{\prime}=e^{m_{i}-m_{i}^{\prime}}\ell_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}e^{S_{ij}-m_{i}^{\prime}}, (2)
ui′\displaystyle u_{i}^{\prime} =emi−mi′​ui+∑j∈𝒥eSi​j−mi′​vj.\displaystyle=e^{m_{i}-m_{i}^{\prime}}u_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}e^{S_{ij}-m_{i}^{\prime}}v_{j}.

After all key tiles 𝒥\mathcal{J} are processed, the worker writes the normalized output oi=ui/ℓio_{i}=u_{i}/\ell_{i} and saves one scalar row log-normalizer per query Li=mi+log⁡ℓiL_{i}=m_{i}+\log\ell_{i}.

In the backward pass, FlashAttention avoids the O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) memory overhead of storing PP by trading on-chip recomputation for reduced HBM traffic. It takes the saved (Q,K,V,O,L)(Q,K,V,O,L) and incoming d​OdO, precomputes Di=⟨d​Oi,oi⟩D_{i}=\langle dO_{i},o_{i}\rangle, and accumulates input gradients across tiles via d​V𝒥+=Pℐ​𝒥⊤​d​OℐdV_{\mathcal{J}}\mathrel{+}=P_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}}^{\top}dO_{\mathcal{I}}, d​K𝒥+=τ​d​Sℐ​𝒥⊤​QℐdK_{\mathcal{J}}\mathrel{+}=\tau dS_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}}^{\top}Q_{\mathcal{I}}, and d​Qℐ+=τ​d​Sℐ​𝒥​K𝒥dQ_{\mathcal{I}}\mathrel{+}=\tau dS_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}}K_{\mathcal{J}} in O⁡(N)O(N) workspace. Because PP was not stored, each tile (ℐ,𝒥)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}) recomputes Sℐ​𝒥S_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} on-chip and uses LℐL_{\mathcal{I}} to reconstruct Pℐ​𝒥P_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} and d​Sℐ​𝒥dS_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} on the fly:

Pℐ​𝒥\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} =exp⁡(Sℐ​𝒥−Lℐ​𝟏⊤),\displaystyle=\exp\!\big(S_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}}-L_{\mathcal{I}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\big), (3)
d​Sℐ​𝒥\displaystyle dS_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} =Pℐ​𝒥⊙(d​Oℐ​V𝒥⊤−Dℐ​𝟏⊤).\displaystyle=P_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}}\odot\big(dO_{\mathcal{I}}V_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}-D_{\mathcal{I}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\big).

3.2 Relative-Position Attention

Relative-position attention extends standard SDPA by incorporating the relative positions of queries and keys directly into their attention scores. Specifically, it adds terms that measure the interaction of the query or key content vectors with a representation of their relative distance and/or assign a scalar bias based on that distance. We express these terms using up to three relation tables with RR rows (r∈{0,…,R−1}r\in\{0,\dots,R-1\}): query- and key-relation vector tables AQ,AK∈ℝR×dA^{Q},A^{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d} with rows (arQ)⊤,(arK)⊤(a^{Q}_{r})^{\top},(a^{K}_{r})^{\top}, and a scalar-bias table b∈ℝRb\in\mathbb{R}^{R}. These tables may be learned directly as parameters or computed by applying learned linear projections to position embeddings. A discrete map ϕ⁡(i,j)∈{0,…,R−1}\phi(i,j)\in\{0,\dots,R-1\} then assigns each query–key pair (i,j)(i,j) to its corresponding relation-row index rr.

For common offset-based mechanisms, ϕ⁡(i,j)\phi(i,j) depends only on the offset δ=i−j\delta=i-j, with rows ordered by increasing δ\delta. Standard mappings fall into three categories:

  • •

    Identity: each integer offset −N+1≤δ≤N−1-N+1\leq\delta\leq N-1 has its own row r=ϕ⁡(i,j)=δ+N−1r=\phi(i,j)=\delta+N-1, so R=2​N−1R=2N-1.

  • •

    Clipped: like identity, but offsets are clamped to [−Δ,Δ][-\Delta,\Delta] for a chosen maximum offset Δ\Delta. In particular, r=ϕ⁡(i,j)=clip⁡(δ,−Δ,Δ)+Δr=\phi(i,j)=\operatorname{clip}(\delta,-\Delta,\Delta)+\Delta and R=2​Δ+1R=2\Delta+1.

  • •

    Bucketed: the most general case: any ϕ⁡(i,j)\phi(i,j) that splits the offsets δ\delta into RR consecutive, ordered buckets.

All such mechanisms share a single canonical score equation that replaces the logits in Eq. 1 with

Si​j=τ⁡(qi⊤​kj+qi⊤​aϕ⁡(i,j)Q+kj⊤​aϕ⁡(i,j)K+bϕ⁡(i,j))+Mi​j,S_{ij}=\tau\left(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}+q_{i}^{\top}a^{Q}_{\phi(i,j)}+k_{j}^{\top}a^{K}_{\phi(i,j)}+b_{\phi(i,j)}\right)+M_{ij}, (4)

where some relation terms can be absent per mechanism. Four widely deployed mechanisms fit this unified view:

  • •

    Shaw (Shaw et al., 2018) uses AQA^{Q}, a clipped map, and sets τ=d−12\tau=d^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

  • •

    Transformer-XL (TXL) (Dai et al., 2019) uses AQA^{Q} and bb, an identity map, and sets τ=d−12\tau=d^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

  • •

    DeBERTa (He et al., 2021; He et al., 2023) uses AQA^{Q}, AKA^{K}, a clipped or bucketed map, and sets τ=(3​d)−12\tau=(3d)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

  • •

    T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) uses only bb under a logarithmic bucketed map.

For notational convenience, we define the query- and key-relation terms for each token and relation row rr, as follows:

Zi​rQ=qi⊤​arQandZj​rK=kj⊤​arK,Z^{Q}_{ir}=q_{i}^{\top}a^{Q}_{r}\quad\text{and}\quad Z^{K}_{jr}=k_{j}^{\top}a^{K}_{r}, (5)

forming the matrices ZQ,ZK∈ℝN×RZ^{Q},Z^{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times R}. For each query–key pair (i,j)(i,j), the corresponding terms in Eq. 4 are then the entries at r=ϕ⁡(i,j)r=\phi(i,j) in ZQZ^{Q} and ZKZ^{K}.

Backward pass

Extending standard attention, the forward pass additionally takes (AQ,AK,b)(A^{Q},A^{K},b) and ϕ\phi, while the backward pass must also compute the table gradients (d​AQ,d​AK,d​b)(dA^{Q},dA^{K},db) alongside the additional positional contributions to d​QdQ and d​KdK. Given the score gradients d​SdS, differentiating through r=ϕ⁡(i,j)r=\phi(i,j) gives:

dZQi​r=τ∑j:ϕ⁡(i,j)=rdSi​janddZKj​r=τ∑i:ϕ⁡(i,j)=rdSi​j.dZ^{Q}_{ir}=\tau\!\!\sum_{j:\,\phi(i,j)=r}\!\!dS_{ij}\quad\text{and}\quad dZ^{K}_{jr}=\tau\!\!\sum_{i:\,\phi(i,j)=r}\!\!dS_{ij}. (6)

3.3 Limitations of Existing Attention Backends

Existing implementations gather or shift copies of the relative-position terms into a dense square matrix before the softmax. Specifically, eager implementations follow one of two strategies, both of which reintroduce quadratic HBM bottlenecks. Naive implementations instantiate aϕ⁡(i,j)Qa^{Q}_{\phi(i,j)} for every (i,j)(i,j) pair, costing O⁡(N2​d)O(N^{2}d) work and O⁡(N2​d)O(N^{2}d) workspace. Preprojected implementations instead compute ZQ,ZK∈ℝN×RZ^{Q},Z^{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times R} in O⁡(N​R​d)O(NRd) work and O⁡(N​R)O(NR) space, then gather or shift them into an N×NN\times N bias matrix. Even with tiling instead of the N×NN\times N bias, the precomputed tables require O⁡(N​R)O(NR) storage, which often include unreachable columns (wasting compute and memory), fetches the same entry multiple times (e.g., when offsets are clipped), and remains quadratic for identity maps.

In the backward pass, tiled execution faces an additional many-to-one reduction bottleneck in Eq. 6. Whenever multiple pairs (i,j)(i,j) map to the same row r=ϕ⁡(i,j)r=\phi(i,j), up to O⁡(N)O(N) keys per query and O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) pairs overall, their score gradients τ​d​Si​j\tau dS_{ij} must be summed into the same d​Zi​rQdZ^{Q}_{ir}, d​Zj​rKdZ^{K}_{jr}, and d​brdb_{r} entries, causing severe atomic contention when accumulated via per-pair updates. While programmable backends such as FlexAttention can avoid the dense N×NN\times N bias through fused per-score callbacks, a scalar callback only sees a single (i,j)(i,j) pair at a time. It cannot change how outer projections are allocated, reuse entries across a tile of pairs sharing the same row rr, or coordinate gradient ownership in backward to avoid atomic additions. Our method overcomes all of these bottlenecks with its relation-aware tiled approach. Derivation of all equations is given in App. B.

4 Method

To address the limitations of Section 3.3, our method brings relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled attention. It computes only the relation projections the tiles read (Section 4.1) and accumulates their gradients by offset (Section 4.2), which together form its forward and backward passes (Section 4.3).

4.1 Reusing Relation Projections

For any offset-based relation map ϕ\phi, each positional term for a query–key pair (i,j)(i,j) depends only on the relation row r=ϕ⁡(i,j)r=\phi(i,j) and either query ii or key jj. Consequently, all N2N^{2} pairwise positional contributions are determined by the N×RN\times R token–relation projections ZQZ^{Q} and ZKZ^{K} (Eq. 5) and the scalar bias b∈ℝRb\in\mathbb{R}^{R}. Rather than expanding these tables into a dense N×NN\times N bias matrix in HBM, our method evaluates them on chip within each attention tile:

Si​j=τ⁡(qi⊤​kj+Zi,ϕ⁡(i,j)Q+Zj,ϕ⁡(i,j)K+bϕ⁡(i,j))+Mi​j.S_{ij}=\tau\bigl(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}+Z^{Q}_{i,\phi(i,j)}+Z^{K}_{j,\phi(i,j)}+b_{\phi(i,j)}\bigr)+M_{ij}. (7)

Each attention logit thus requires at most three scalar lookups from ZQZ^{Q}, ZKZ^{K}, and bb rather than a dd-dimensional dot product. We next eliminate the two remaining bottlenecks identified in Section 3.3 – computing unreachable projection columns and performing redundant elementwise lookups.

Reachable Projection Ranges

Although an identity map defines 2​N−12N-1 relation rows, any single query ii only attends to NN keys. It thus accesses NN contiguous offsets δ∈[i−N+1,i]\delta\in[i-N+1,i], leaving the remaining N−1N-1 rows of AQA^{Q} unused. To omit these unreachable projections while preserving batched matrix multiplications, our method partitions QQ into contiguous groups QgQ_{g} of GG queries. Because consecutive queries access overlapping offsets, an entire group QgQ_{g} reaches a contiguous range ΩgQ={g​G,…,g​G+N+G−2}\Omega^{Q}_{g}=\{gG,\ldots,gG+N+G-2\} of only N+G−1N+G-1 rows, reducing overhead to only G−1G-1 additional rows. Our method projects each QgQ_{g} onto AΩgQQA^{Q}_{\Omega^{Q}_{g}} (and analogically for KgK_{g} and AΩgKKA^{K}_{\Omega^{K}_{g}}) as a single dense matrix product. For N≫GN\gg G, this restriction nearly halves both projection work and HBM storage while remaining exact. The scalar bias bb requires no projection and is left unrestricted.

Constant-Range Reuse

For clipped and bucketed maps with a small saturation limit Δ≪N\Delta\ll N, individual token groups already span nearly all RR relation rows, offering limited savings from range restriction. Instead, these maps saturate outside the diagonal band |δ|<Δ|\delta|<\Delta, mapping all offsets δ≥Δ\delta\geq\Delta to row r=R−1r=R-1 and all δ≤−Δ\delta\leq-\Delta to row r=0r=0. To handle bucketed maps in the same way, our method expands their RR buckets into 2​Δ+12\Delta+1 rows by duplicating each bucket across the offsets it covers, replacing index lookups with clipping. In any tile where |δ|≥Δ|\delta|\geq\Delta, all pairs map to the same row rr. Our method therefore loads a single entry per query (Zi​rQZ^{Q}_{ir}), one per key (Zj​rKZ^{K}_{jr}), and one bias brb_{r}, broadcasting them across the tile. Only pairs in the diagonal band |δ|<Δ|\delta|<\Delta require individual lookups, and their fraction (2​Δ−1)/N(2\Delta-1)/N approaches zero as NN grows. Under causal masking (j≤ij\leq i), the situation is similar, but queries access only offsets δ≥0\delta\geq 0 and saturate only for δ≥Δ\delta\geq\Delta.

4.2 Atomic-free Relation Gradient Accumulation

In the backward pass, accumulating score gradients τ​d​Si​j\tau\,dS_{ij} directly into d​ZQdZ^{Q} and d​ZKdZ^{K} causes atomic contention whenever multiple pairs map to the same relation row rr. However, while a fixed query ii may map many keys jj to the same row rr, each key corresponds to a unique offset δ=i−j\delta=i-j. Building on the standard two-pass backward schedule (Triton Contributors, 2024), our method assigns each query tile to a single thread block and accumulates its gradients by offset δ\delta into d​Z~Qd\tilde{Z}^{Q} rather than by row rr. A symmetric pass over key tiles accumulates d​Z~Kd\tilde{Z}^{K}. Because each entry has a single writer, this schedule eliminates all O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) atomic additions and fixes the summation order, ensuring determinism.

Local Boundary Sums

Similar to the forward pass, writing a separate gradient entry for every offset δ\delta is unnecessary in the saturated regions. Since all δ≥Δ\delta\geq\Delta map to row R−1R-1 and all δ≤−Δ\delta\leq-\Delta map to row 00, each thread block maintains two on-chip running sums per token, one for each boundary row, and writes them to HBM only once. Combined with the reachable ranges ΩgQ\Omega^{Q}_{g} and ΩgK\Omega^{K}_{g}, each token stores at most min⁡(N+G−1, 2​Δ+1)\min(N+G-1,\,2\Delta+1) gradient entries (identity maps have Δ=N−1\Delta=N-1) instead of one per offset, 2​N−12N-1. As in Section 4.1, this nearly halves the gradient buffer for identity maps (N≫GN\gg G), while for clipped and bucketed maps the fraction (2​Δ+1)/(2​N−1)(2\Delta+1)/(2N-1) approaches zero as NN grows.

Relation-Row Reduction

The stored offset gradients directly yield d​ZQdZ^{Q} and d​ZKdZ^{K} (Eq. 6). For identity and clipped maps, each stored column already corresponds to its own row rr (d​Z~Q=d​ZQd\tilde{Z}^{Q}=dZ^{Q}). For bucketed maps, the duplicated columns of each bucket are summed back into that bucket’s row in a fixed, deterministic order. The remaining gradients then reduce to matrix products, as in Section 3.2. For Δ≪N\Delta\ll N, these reductions require O⁡(N​Δ​d)O(N\Delta d) work rather than O⁡(N2​d)O(N^{2}d) for per-pair accumulation. Our method uses this atomic-free path whenever each row rr spans contiguous offsets, and falls back to atomic additions otherwise.

4.3 Complete Algorithm

We now compose the end-to-end algorithm, designing both the forward and backward passes in a tiled manner.

4.3.1 Forward algorithm

To avoid materializing dense attention matrices in HBM, our method streams query and key tiles through on-chip SRAM, similarly carrying over FlashAttention’s tiled schedule, which remains applicable as each score tile Sℐ​𝒥S_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} depends only on the preprojected relation entries of its own queries ℐ\mathcal{I} and keys 𝒥\mathcal{J}. Algorithm 1 extends standard tiled attention in two places: precomputing the group projections before the tiled loop (lines 1–4) and adding the relative-position terms on chip within it (lines 11–17).

Inside the inner loop, the edge indices of a score tile determine its extreme offsets δmin\delta_{\min} and δmax\delta_{\max}, so two comparisons suffice to check whether the tile saturates (lines 11–12). Saturated tiles load and broadcast one entry per query and key (line 13), whereas tiles intersecting the diagonal band perform per-score lookups (line 15). We align the group size with the maximum tile size, chosen to be G=128G=128, ensuring that every tile reads its projections from a single group with only 1.6%1.6\% column overhead at N=8​KN=8\text{K} tokens. When a single group already reaches all RR rows, as for clipped and bucketed maps with Δ≪N\Delta\ll N, our method uses one group for the whole sequence. By default, the forward pass saves ZQZ^{Q} and ZKZ^{K} in HBM for the backward pass, though they can instead be recomputed during backpropagation to reduce activation memory, which would, however, double projection work.

4.3.2 Complete Backward Algorithm

The backward pass (Algorithm 2) executes a query-parallel pass for d​QdQ and d​Z~Qd\tilde{Z}^{Q}, followed by a key-parallel pass for d​KdK, d​VdV, and d​Z~Kd\tilde{Z}^{K}. Both passes recompute Sℐ​𝒥S_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} as in the forward pass (line 7), recover Pℐ​𝒥P_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} and d​Sℐ​𝒥dS_{\mathcal{I}\mathcal{J}} via Eq. 3, and accumulate τ​d​Si​j\tau\,dS_{ij} by offset with on-chip boundary sums for |δ|≥Δ|\delta|\geq\Delta (lines 10 and 22). Once the tiled loops finish, lines 26–30 reduce duplicated bucket columns into d​ZQ,d​ZKdZ^{Q},dZ^{K} when applicable and compute the remaining gradients via matrix products (Section 3.2).

4.3.3 Implementation

We implement our method in Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) as a drop-in replacement for relative-position attention, with adapters for Hugging Face and NeMo models that require no weight modifications. Each call dispatches a kernel specialized at compile time to the active relation terms, map type and Δ\Delta, masking, sequence packing, dropout, precision, and tile sizes, avoiding runtime branching and any overhead from disabled terms. Tile sizes are selected by sequence-length bucket from lookup tables tuned offline per GPU architecture, falling back to a hardware resource heuristic when no table entry exists. Similarly, the saturation check (lines 11–12 of Algorithm 1) splits each tile’s inner loop into three contiguous ranges on the host rather than branching per tile. Sequence lengths remain runtime arguments so lengths within a bucket share compiled kernels, with an optional precompilation step to warm the compiler cache. Users can trade compute for memory by selecting whether the forward pass saves ZQZ^{Q} and ZKZ^{K} in HBM or recomputes them during backpropagation. Finally, all kernels are custom PyTorch operators compatible with torch.compile (Ansel et al., 2024).

5 Evaluation

In this section, we present the empirical evaluation of our method. We first describe our experimental setup, including the target mechanisms and hardware, alongside the baselines we compare against (Section 5.1). We then evaluate our method at two levels. At the attention-block level we benchmark forward and backward throughput and memory footprints (Section 5.2). Second, we apply our method in end-to-end tasks, including training and inference, while comparing downstream task quality across three production workloads (Section 5.3). Finally, we isolate and measure the impact of each algorithmic optimization of our method in ablation studies (Section 5.4).

5.1 Experimental Setup

Mechanisms

We evaluate the four mechanisms of Section 3.2 with the maps their models use. Shaw clips offsets, as in the w2v-BERT encoders of SeamlessM4T (Barrault et al., 2023), here at Δ=256\Delta=256. TXL uses the identity map, as in the FastConformer encoders of Canary and Parakeet (Rekesh et al., 2023; Sekoyan et al., 2025). DeBERTa uses 256 logarithmic buckets up to distance 512, as in DeBERTa-v3 (He et al., 2023), and T5 uses 32 bidirectional buckets up to distance 128, as in the original T5 (Raffel et al., 2020).

Baselines

We compare to general and mechanism-specific implementations in Table 1, from their official repositories, Hugging Face Transformers (Wolf et al., 2020), or NeMo, with every dense bias built by the models’ attention modules, as in practice. We call those without our decomposition production systems. Compiled PyTorch, FlexAttention, and our method run under torch.compile, FA4 and FlashInfer under their own JIT compilers.

Correctness

To ensure exactness, we validate every output and gradient tensor against an independent FP32 reference, computed eagerly from the relation equations by gathering the relation vector for each query–key pair. An implementation passes if, when cast to FP32, each of its output and gradient tensors is elementwise within 5% relative and 0.03 absolute error, or has a relative ℓ2\ell_{2} error within eight rounding units of the target data type (0.78% for FP16). We mark systems that fail this check with † in Table 1. The full results, presented in App. F and G, mark them with † as well. Our method always passes this check.

Hardware and software

Unless noted otherwise, we run all experiments on a single NVIDIA H200 SXM GPU using CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.14.1, Triton 3.8.0, FA4 4.0.0b33, FlashInfer 0.7.2, and FlashDeBERTa 0.0.7.

5.2 Attention-Level Performance

We benchmark one attention layer, from QQ, KK, VV and the relation tables to OO and, backward, to their gradients.

Setup

Following FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024), we fix a budget of 16K tokens and sweep NN from 128 to 8K tokens with batch size B=16​K/NB=16\text{K}/N, H=12H=12 heads of dimension d=64d=64, FP16, and bidirectional attention. We time forward passes and backward passes (with stored relevant forward pass values) and report throughput as useful FLOPs over latency, crediting every system the same work, so throughput ratios are latency ratios. Peak memory is recorded as the device memory allocated beyond the inputs. Appendix D details the FLOP count and the timing protocol.

Throughput

Figure 2 compares our method with the fastest system of each kind. Our method outperforms every production system at every length except T5’s backward pass at 128 and 256 tokens (0.75–0.82×\times), where our setup overhead dominates. For Shaw, DeBERTa, and T5, its lead increases as sequences grow, to 1.8–6.4×\times in the forward and 2.0–21×\times in the backward pass at 8K tokens. This is expected, since every production baseline either reads a dense N×NN\times N bias or obtains its relation terms score by score, while our method instead reads one entry per query and per key wherever |δ|≥Δ|\delta|\geq\Delta, so its share of individual lookups vanishes as NN grows. TXL gains less (1.4–2.4×\times), as its identity map gives every offset its own row and keeps the projections quadratic in NN for all systems, including our method. We note that for DeBERTa’s backward pass, every production system fails our FP32 check from 4K tokens (Table 1), while our method remains exact. Full results are in Table 11 in App. F.

Memory footprint

Table 3 compares the peak memory of our method with eager PyTorch, the leanest production baseline, and the leanest engine running our decomposition at 128 and 8K tokens, with full results in Table 12 in App. F. At 128 tokens, our method is on par with the leanest system, needing the least memory or within a few tens of MiB of it. In terms of memory, systems that build the dense bias keep growing with NN, and at 8K tokens, our method needs 2.9–128×\times less forward and 1.4–54×\times less backward memory than the leanest production system. Every system’s footprint grows monotonically with NN, so these findings stay consistent with sequence length. The one exception is DeBERTa’s forward pass, where the inference-only GLiNER4j recomputes the relation products in every tile instead of storing projections. However, as shown in Fig. 2, this comes at a significant throughput cost, where our method outperforms it 3.7×3.7\times.

Is the relation decomposition enough?

Our decomposition (Eq. 7) also fits the per-score callbacks of programmable engines. We thus compare integrating only this component against our method as a whole. In the forward pass, this lifts the engines above their dense-bias form at long sequences. Our method still stays 1.1–2.2×\times faster at 8K tokens (Table 2). In the backward pass, the gap widens to 1.7–228×\times, because the engines accumulate the table gradients with an atomic addition per score. Atomic contention also costs memory: on every mechanism but T5, the engines’ backward pass needs at least as much as the backward pass of our method.

Different GPU architectures

On Blackwell and Ampere architectures, namely RTX PRO 6000 and RTX A6000, our method generalizes well, as it keeps its lead over the production systems at 8K tokens (Table 2), with the same pattern as on the H200: the largest gains on Shaw, and the smallest on TXL. We provide the full results in App. G.

5.3 End-to-End Performance

To show practical efficiency, we apply our method to three released models, targeting speech transcription and long-audio fine-tuning with FastConformer’s TXL attention, and long-document classification with DeBERTa-v3’s disentangled attention. All experiments were run on one H200 in BF16 mixed precision, with the software and recipes in App. D. We report the median time, excluding the one-time compilation and autotuning of our method, which takes under 3 minutes and is cached afterwards. For speech, we also report the word error rate (WER) and the inverse real-time factor (RTFx) (Srivastav et al., 2026), the seconds of audio transcribed per wall-clock second.

Transcription with Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3

Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (Sekoyan et al., 2025) pairs a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) decoder (Xu et al., 2023), and our method replaces only the encoder’s attention. We transcribe the TED-LIUM 3 test set (Hernandez et al., 2018) in NeMo (Kuchaiev et al., 2019), once as short segments and once as whole talks of up to 25 minutes (Table 4). We compare against NeMo’s production attention paths, native and SDPA (App. D). Our method matches the WER of native attention, making it a drop-in replacement for trained models. Since the rest of the model runs unchanged, its gain is bounded by the share of time spent in attention, unlike in the isolated layer (Section 5.2). On short segments, this share is small, and our method is 1.2×\times faster than SDPA. On whole talks, attention dominates, and our method nearly doubles throughput while needing a fifth of the memory of native attention. In fine-tuning, the transducer loss adds an overhead that dominates each step, so our method brings no speedup at any length.

Fine-tuning Canary-1B-v2 on long audio

Canary-1B-v2 (Sekoyan et al., 2025) pairs a FastConformer encoder with a Transformer autoregressive decoder. Due to the autoregressive decoder, our method brings little or no speedup in token generation, and helps only during prefill, i.e., the encoder pass, which takes at most a quarter of the inference time, and under 5% from 5-minute windows on. To test training, we fine-tune all its parameters on TED-LIUM 3 talks cut into windows of 30 seconds to 18 minutes, and test on windows of the same length (Table 5). Training losses match NeMo’s SDPA path at every window both run, and test WER agrees up to 5-minute windows, beyond which a few long recordings dominate the differences (App. D). The gain again follows attention’s share of each step, so our method speeds up training steps by 1.09–1.36×\times, more for longer windows. SDPA runs out of memory from 15-minute windows, while our method fits both by recomputing its projections in the backward pass, scaling to longer contexts.

Long-document classification with DeBERTa-v3

Finally, for text, following Condevaux & Harispe (2023), we fine-tune DeBERTa-v3-base to classify BIGPATENT (Sharma et al., 2019) patents into nine CPC sections, with inputs truncated to 512, 2K, or 4K tokens, and compare with a Transformers pipeline (Table 6). Both reach the same test accuracy within 0.3 points, and longer inputs improve it. Our method more than doubles training speed from 2K tokens on. Its peak memory also stops growing at 2K tokens, while Transformers’ reaches almost four times as much at 4K.

5.4 Ablation Studies

To isolate the efficacy of each part of our contribution, Table 7 switches off one component of our method at a time, and registers the memory and efficiency tradeoff. Appendix E further reports the results on every mechanism and the HBM traffic.

Two methods carry most of the speedup. Without atomic-free gradients, the backward pass is 2.9–4.4×\times slower, needs 1.8–2.6×\times the memory, and loses determinism. The decomposition engines use atomics, hence their backward gap in Section 5.2. Without projections, every tile computes its own relation products, which slows the forward pass by 2.0–2.9×\times and the backward pass even more, but needs only 0.19–0.43×\times the memory, the same tradeoff GLiNER4j makes.

The other methods are more targeted, with considerable gains of up to 1.3×\times in time or 1.5×\times in memory on the maps they serve (Table 10). Reachable ranges save memory, mainly on TXL’s identity map, while constant-range reuse speeds up the clipped and bucketed maps. Bucket copies add further speed at a memory cost. Finally, recomputing the projections instead of retaining them cuts memory to 0.42–0.50×\times for a 1.1×\times slowdown, which is how our method is able to fit Canary’s longest windows (Section 5.3).

6 Limitations

While our method resolves the main bottlenecks of relative-position attention, several limitations remain. First, identity maps such as Transformer-XL’s assign a distinct relation row to every offset, so their projection work and space remain quadratic in sequence length. Computing the projections inside each tile instead makes the space linear but is 2.0–2.9×\times slower in the forward pass (Table 7). Second, maps whose relation rows do not cover consecutive offsets fall back to FP32 atomic accumulation, which is slower and not deterministic, although every evaluated mechanism avoids it. Third, our method favors generality across mechanisms, maps, and GPUs over hardware specialization. It autotunes its tile sizes but uses no architecture-specific primitives such as warp specialization or asynchronous bulk transfers (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026), which could yield further speedups and which we leave as future work.

7 Conclusion

We presented an exact tiled algorithm that unifies and accelerates additive relative-position attention. By restricting relation projections to reachable ranges, reusing entries across constant-offset tiles, and accumulating gradients by offset without atomics, our method removes the dense bias of existing backends, with its memory and bandwidth costs, and keeps gradients deterministic for identity, clipped, and bucketed maps. Across mechanisms and GPUs, our method is a drop-in replacement for long-context training and inference in production models, so these mechanisms no longer need to be substituted for efficiency.

Appendix A Notation

Table 8 lists the symbols of Sections 3 and 4 and App. B. We consider one sequence and one attention head, and all indices are zero-based. Symbols local to a single proof are defined where they are used.

Appendix B Gradient Derivations and Tiling Correctness

This appendix derives the gradients of relative-position attention (Section B.1) and shows that the tiled passes of our method compute them exactly (Section B.2). All claims hold in exact arithmetic; in floating point, the tiled passes only fix the order of the same sums.

Setup

We consider one head and write ℒ\mathcal{L} for the training loss and d​X=∂ℒ/∂XdX=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial X. By Eq. 5, the canonical scores (Eq. 4) equal

Si​j=τ⁡(qi⊤​kj+Zi​rQ+Zj​rK+br)+Mi​j,S_{ij}=\tau\bigl(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}+Z^{Q}_{ir}+Z^{K}_{jr}+b_{r}\bigr)+M_{ij}, (8)

with r=ϕ⁡(i,j)r=\phi(i,j), P=softmaxrow⁡(S)P=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S), and O=P​VO=PV. Absent terms are zero. We write [⋅][\cdot] for the indicator of a condition and assume each query has at least one unmasked key. For offset-based maps we write ϕ​(i,j)=ϕ¯​(i−j)\phi(i,j)=\bar{\phi}(i-j), where ϕ¯\bar{\phi} is nondecreasing and saturates at Δ\Delta (Section 3.2).

B.1 Gradients

Lemma B.1 (Softmax backward).

Let d​Pi​j=⟨d​Oi,vj⟩dP_{ij}=\langle dO_{i},v_{j}\rangle and Di=⟨d​Oi,oi⟩D_{i}=\langle dO_{i},o_{i}\rangle. Then

d​V=P⊤​d​O,d​Si​j=Pi​j​(d​Pi​j−Di).dV=P^{\top}dO,\qquad dS_{ij}=P_{ij}\,(dP_{ij}-D_{i}).
Proof.

Step 1. Since oi=∑jPi​j​vjo_{i}=\sum_{j}P_{ij}v_{j} is linear in PP and VV, we get d​Pi​j=⟨d​Oi,vj⟩dP_{ij}=\langle dO_{i},v_{j}\rangle and d​vj=∑iPi​j​d​Oidv_{j}=\sum_{i}P_{ij}\,dO_{i}, that is, d​V=P⊤​d​OdV=P^{\top}dO.

Step 2. Row ii of PP depends only on row ii of SS, with ∂Pi​t/∂Si​j=Pi​t([t=j]−Pi​j)\partial P_{it}/\partial S_{ij}=P_{it}([t=j]-P_{ij}).

Step 3. By the chain rule,

d​Si​j\displaystyle dS_{ij} =∑tdPi​tPi​t([t=j]−Pi​j)\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{t}dP_{it}P_{it}([t=j]-P_{ij})
=Pi​j​(d​Pi​j−∑tPi​t​d​Pi​t).\displaystyle=P_{ij}\bigl(dP_{ij}-\textstyle\sum_{t}P_{it}\,dP_{it}\bigr).

Step 4. By Step 1, ∑tPi​t​d​Pi​t=⟨d​Oi,∑tPi​t​vt⟩=⟨d​Oi,oi⟩=Di\sum_{t}P_{it}\,dP_{it}=\langle dO_{i},\sum_{t}P_{it}v_{t}\rangle=\langle dO_{i},o_{i}\rangle=D_{i}. ∎

Masked pairs have Pi​j=0P_{ij}=0 and thus d​Si​j=0dS_{ij}=0, so they contribute nothing to any gradient below.

Lemma B.2 (Score gradients).

Treating Q,K,ZQ,ZK,bQ,K,Z^{Q},Z^{K},b in Eq. 8 as independent inputs, their gradients are τ​d​S​K\tau\,dS\,K for QQ, τ​d​S⊤​Q\tau\,dS^{\top}Q for KK, and Eq. 6 for ZQ,ZK,bZ^{Q},Z^{K},b.

Proof.

Step 1. Si​jS_{ij} is affine in each input, with partial derivatives

∂Si​j/∂qi′\displaystyle\partial S_{ij}/\partial q_{i^{\prime}} =τ[i′=i]kj,\displaystyle=\tau[i^{\prime}=i]\,k_{j},
∂Si​j/∂Zi′​rQ\displaystyle\partial S_{ij}/\partial Z^{Q}_{i^{\prime}r} =τ[i′=i][ϕ(i,j)=r],\displaystyle=\tau[i^{\prime}=i]\,[\phi(i,j)=r],
∂Si​j/∂Zj′​rK\displaystyle\partial S_{ij}/\partial Z^{K}_{j^{\prime}r} =τ[j′=j][ϕ(i,j)=r],\displaystyle=\tau[j^{\prime}=j]\,[\phi(i,j)=r],
∂Si​j/∂br\displaystyle\partial S_{ij}/\partial b_{r} =τ[ϕ(i,j)=r],\displaystyle=\tau[\phi(i,j)=r],

and symmetrically for kj′k_{j^{\prime}}.

Step 2. Each gradient is ∑i,jd​Si​j\sum_{i,j}dS_{ij} times the matching partial derivative. The indicators [i′=i][i^{\prime}=i] and [j′=j][j^{\prime}=j] remove one sum, and [ϕ(i,j)=r][\phi(i,j)=r] restricts the other to the pairs mapped to row rr, which gives Eq. 6. ∎

Each pair (i,j)(i,j) thus adds τ​d​Si​j\tau\,dS_{ij} to exactly one entry of each of d​ZQdZ^{Q}, d​ZKdZ^{K}, and d​bdb, namely row ϕ⁡(i,j)\phi(i,j). We define d​ZQdZ^{Q} and d​ZKdZ^{K} by Eq. 6 even when AQA^{Q} or AKA^{K} is absent.

With ZQ=Q​(AQ)⊤Z^{Q}=Q(A^{Q})^{\top} and ZK=K​(AK)⊤Z^{K}=K(A^{K})^{\top},

Proposition B.9 (Atomic-free accumulation).

Let ϕ\phi be offset-based, and let each block of the query-owned pass of Algorithm 2 own one query tile ℐ\mathcal{I}.

Proof.

Step 1. The map j↦i−jj\mapsto i-j is injective, and its image over j∈{0,…,N−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\} is {i−N+1,…,i}\{i-N+1,\ldots,i\}. Reindexing the sum over jj in Eq. 6 by δ\delta gives (a).

Algorithm 2 returns the exact gradients d​Q,d​K,d​V,d​AQ,d​AK,d​bdQ,dK,dV,dA^{Q},dA^{K},db of Lemma B.3.

Appendix C Kernel and Algorithm Details

Section 4.3.3 summarizes our implementation. Here, we detail how our method maps Algorithms 1 and 2 onto kernels, how it reduces the relation gradients deterministically, how it stores relation projections in half precision, and which inputs and tile sizes its kernels support.

Kernel structure

Table 9 lists the kernels of our method in launch order, with the lines of Algorithms 1 and 2 that each one runs. The forward pass first projects every query group and key group onto its reachable range and stores the preprojected relation entries in HBM. The attention kernel then runs the tiled loop and writes OO and LL. The backward pass computes DD and runs the query-parallel pass, whose gradient entries are reduced into d​QdQ, d​AQdA^{Q}, and d​bdb before the key-parallel pass starts. Both passes can therefore write their gradient entries into the same buffer. The key-parallel pass and its reduction then produce d​KdK, d​VdV, and d​AKdA^{K}. If the forward pass does not save ZQZ^{Q} and ZKZ^{K}, the backward pass recomputes them with the projection kernel before it starts. When both AQA^{Q} and bb are present, the projection kernel adds bb into the stored ZQZ^{Q}, so each score reads two entries instead of three. Bucket copies (line 1) run before the projection and copy the rows of the tables rather than the columns of the projections, A~Q=E​AQ\tilde{A}^{Q}=EA^{Q}, which gives the same Z~Q=Q​(A~Q)⊤=ZQ​E⊤\tilde{Z}^{Q}=Q(\tilde{A}^{Q})^{\top}=Z^{Q}E^{\top}.

Deterministic table gradients

Each table gradient is a sum over all tokens. Our method splits the tokens into chunks cc and computes d​AQ=∑c(d​ZcQ)⊤​QcdA^{Q}=\sum_{c}(dZ^{Q}_{c})^{\top}Q_{c}, and likewise d​AKdA^{K} and d​bdb, in two kernels. In the first, each thread block computes the term of one chunk and writes it to HBM in FP32. In the second, these terms are summed in a fixed order. For bucketed maps, the gradients of the copied rows are then summed back into their buckets, d​AQ=E⊤​d​A~QdA^{Q}=E^{\top}d\tilde{A}^{Q}, also in a fixed order. No gradient is accumulated atomically, so the backward pass is deterministic.

Atomic fallback

Accumulating gradients by offset (Section 4.2) requires each relation row to cover one contiguous interval of offsets. This holds for identity, clipped, and bucketed maps, and our method checks it once per map on the host. Maps that fail it fall back to kernels that accumulate their relation gradients with FP32 atomic additions. Examples are maps that give δ\delta and −δ-\delta the same row, or maps that depend on more than the offset.

Half-precision numerics

Inputs may be in FP16, BF16, or FP32. The online softmax uses base-2 exponentials, with log2⁡e\log_{2}e folded into τ\tau, and its statistics, the accumulators, and the boundary sums stay in FP32 on chip. In HBM, the gradient entries use the input precision. The relation projections use FP16 for both FP16 and BF16 inputs. BF16 gives up three mantissa bits for a wider range, so FP16 stores the projections with an eight times smaller rounding error. For BF16 inputs, the projections are clamped to the FP16 range of ±65504\pm 65504, so that an outlier cannot overflow to infinity.

Masks, packing, and dropout

The kernels support padding masks, causal masks, and packed variable-length sequences, in which each thread block processes a query tile of one sequence. Attention dropout draws its mask from a counter-based random number generator inside the kernels, so the backward pass regenerates the mask of the forward pass instead of storing it.

Specialization and tuning

The sequence-length buckets end at 64, 128, 384, 512, 768, 1K, 2K, 4K, and 8K tokens, and longer sequences use the 8K bucket. Besides the specializations of Section 4.3.3, each kernel is compiled separately for lengths that are and are not a multiple of 16, so a bucket needs at most two compilations per kernel. For multiples of 16, Triton can use wider memory accesses, so our model adapters pad each sequence to a multiple of 16 tokens and mask the padding. For the same reason, each group’s range of projection columns starts and ends on a multiple of 16. Our lookup tables cover compute capabilities 8.0, 8.6, and 9.0 (A100, RTX A6000, and H100 or H200), with one entry per kernel, precision, head dimension, bucket, and set of relation terms. The hardware resource heuristic starts from a 64×6464\times 64 tile and shrinks it until its estimated registers and shared memory fit the GPU. Instead of both, our method can autotune each kernel at run time over a short list of candidate tile sizes, once per bucket. All measurements in Section 5 use autotuning, which the end-to-end runs complete in the precompilation step before timing. The exception is the ablation that computes the projections inside each tile (Table 7), which uses its fastest fixed tile sizes.

Appendix D Additional Experimental Details

Kernel benchmarks

A forward pass is credited 4​B​H​N2​d4BHN^{2}d FLOPs for its two attention GEMMs plus 2​B​H​N​R​d2BHNRd for each relation projection over RR table rows: one for Shaw and TXL (AQA^{Q}), two for DeBERTa (AQA^{Q} and AKA^{K}), and none for T5. A backward pass is credited twice as much, for its four attention GEMMs and the two gradient GEMMs of each projection. FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) instead credits 2.5 times the forward FLOPs, counting the recomputed scores, which we leave out because not every system recomputes them. Each measurement runs in a fresh process with triton.testing.do_bench, which flushes the L2 cache before each sample. After 50ms of warmup, we report the median of at least ten timed runs. Compilation and autotuning happen before timing and are excluded. Systems under torch.compile use its max-autotune mode with static shapes and without CUDA graphs. Within each mechanism and length, the systems run in a random order, and we record GPU clocks, power, and temperature instead of locking the clocks. The RTX PRO 6000 and RTX A6000 use the same software as the H200.

End-to-end software

The speech models run in NeMo 3.0.0 on PyTorch 2.9.1 and CUDA 12.8, and DeBERTa on the software stack of Section 5.1.

Parakeet transcription

The test set has 1,155 segments and 11 talks of up to ∼25{\sim}25 minutes, which we transcribe one at a time. We report word error rate (WER) after Whisper’s text normalization (Radford et al., 2023), for which NVIDIA’s model card reports 2.75% (NVIDIA, 2025), and inverse real-time factor (RTFx), the audio seconds processed per wall-clock second. NeMo’s FlexAttention path captures sequence-length-dependent index arithmetic and bias tensors in its score_mod closure, so each new input length triggers a torch.compile recompilation that erases any speedup, and running it uncompiled falls back to a much slower unfused implementation.

Canary fine-tuning

We fine-tune on 100 hours of TED-LIUM 3 training talks, cut into windows of at most 30 seconds and 2, 5, 9, 15, and 18 minutes, for 3 epochs with about 540 seconds of audio per step. Final-epoch training losses match within 0.4% at every window both attentions run. As Whisper does, we decode transcripts that fall into repetition loops again in shorter pieces. From 9-minute windows on, such loops affect one or two long recordings per window, and these recordings account for the remaining WER differences.

DeBERTa fine-tuning

The patent data has 25,000 training, 5,000 validation, and 5,000 test documents of 3,900 tokens on average. We train for 3 epochs with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) at a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, 10% linear warmup, weight decay 0.01, and 16 patents per step in 4K-token micro-batches, and report test accuracy at the best validation epoch. Macro-F1 agrees within 0.3 points from 2K tokens and differs by +1.3 points at 512 tokens. Condevaux & Harispe (2023) report 66.6 micro-F1 and 61.8 macro-F1 for RoBERTa on this task.

Appendix E Additional Ablations

Table 10 gives every method of Table 7 for each mechanism and pass.

HBM traffic

We also count the bytes each pass reads from and writes to HBM with Nsight Compute, on an H100 at 4K tokens, with each method switched off (Table 10). Atomic accumulation adds the traffic of full FP32 gradient buffers to the backward pass, 1.3–3.1×\times that of our method and 3.1×\times on TXL, whose identity map has the most entries. Without reachable ranges, TXL stores and rereads projections for every offset instead of only the reachable ones and moves 1.4×\times the data, while DeBERTa, whose groups already reach nearly all rows, stays at 1.0×\times. Constant-range reuse leaves the traffic unchanged at 0.95–1.0×\times: without it, a saturated tile rereads the same entry for every score, and these repeated reads hit in on-chip caches, so its speedup comes from fewer loads and index computations rather than from fewer bytes. Bucket copies store a projection column per offset instead of per bucket, which raises DeBERTa’s traffic by 1.2–1.8×\times. Computing the relation products inside each tile reads no stored projections, so Shaw and TXL move only 0.044–0.19×\times the data, but every tile recomputes them.

Appendix F Detailed Results on the H200

Tables 11 and 12 give the throughput and peak memory of every system behind Fig. 2 and Table 3 at every sequence length. FlexAttention, FA4, and FlashInfer without our decomposition run on the model’s dense bias.

Memory across lengths

The footprint of our method stops growing beyond 1K tokens for Shaw, DeBERTa, and T5, and grows only with the projections for TXL (Table 12). GLiNER4j’s lower forward memory on DeBERTa comes from recomputing the relation products in every tile instead of storing projections. The projections ablation (Table 7) shows this trade within our method: less memory, but a 2.0–2.9×\times slower forward pass.

Appendix G Results on Other GPUs

Tables 13 and 14 give the throughput of every system on the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and the RTX A6000 at every sequence length, as Table 11 does on the H200.

Appendix H Code and Data Availability

We will open-source the code of our method, our benchmark and end-to-end scripts, and all result files. The result files record every measurement together with its software versions, tile sizes, and GPU telemetry, and our scripts generate every result in this paper from them. The code includes tests that compare every output and gradient with an FP32 reference under padding, packing, causal masks, dropout, and each input precision. All models and datasets we use are public (App. D).
